newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit hits 3-year low, more downside seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit hits 3-year low, more downside seen.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit continued its slide, hitting a three-year low against the dollar on Friday, and foreign exchange dealers said more downside was likely in the short term.
The Malaysian currency fell to 2.6100 to a dollar, its weakest level since July 1994. By 0846 GMT, it was at 2.6060/90.
The ringgit has fallen more than three percent this week as speculators found a fresh target after attacking the Thai baht and Philippine peso.
"Speculative funds are still behind the ringgit selling," said a dealer with a large Malaysian bank. "I'm not surprised if the dollar goes above 2.61 later in the day."
Dealers said the next target for dollar/ringgit is at 2.6150, which is five percent appreciation from 2.4900 -- the lowest point before the run-up.

"I think 2.6000 will be the new base for dollar/ringgit," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. "All the other currencies in the region are falling, including the Singapore dollar. So it's no surprise to see ringgit coming off."
Dealers said there was talk that funds would try to push the dollar/ringgit rate to 2.6500.
Dealers said the central Bank Negara was not seen in the market despite the dollar's climb beyond the 2.6000 mark. It was earlier said to have been holding the rate at that level.
Dealers said the ringgit's undertone remains bearish following a perceived change in stance by Malaysian authorities.
Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday that Malaysia would allow the exchange rate to be determined by market forces.
The statement was interpreted to mean Bank Negara had given up its strategy of vigorously defending the ringgit at a particular level and was willing to tolerate further ringgit weakness.
The central bank had earlier this month spent more than $1 billion to defend the ringgit from speculative attack.

On Friday, when asked by reporters why Bank Negara had subsequently stayed out of the foreign exchange market despite the ringgit's fall to a three-year low, Anwar said: "What makes you think that 2.60 is not reasonable?"
He added it could go to a four-year low, but when asked if he was serious, he said: "I'm smiling, that means I'm joking."
The ringgit was at around 2.78 to the dollar in early 1994.
